newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian labour leader challenges conviction.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian labour leader challenges conviction.

text.p: Jailed Indonesian labour leader Muchtar Pakpahan made a rare public appearance in court on Thursday as part of a tangled web of legal moves in which the Supreme Court reversed one of its own rulings.
In a separate case, Pakpahan faces a subversion charge carrying a maximum penalty of death for his activities as leader of the independent Indonesian Labour Welfare Union (SBSI).
He has been in hospital since March, although the exact nature of his illness is unclear. International labour leaders and the U.S. government have offered to pay for his treatment abroad.

The 43-year-old activist was sentenced in 1994 to three years in jail for inciting anti-Chinese riots in which one person died in the northern Sumatra trading city of Medan in April that year after a labour strike.
The High Court in Medan later increased the sentence to four years, but the Supreme Court in Jakarta freed him in April 1995 and overturned his conviction in September the same year.

In an unprecedented move last year that astounded the legal profession, the Supreme Court reversed itself and reinstated his jail term after he was arrested on the subversion charge following July 1996 riots in Jakarta.

In a 90-minute opening statement on Thursday, read mostly by his team of lawyers in the main chamber of the East Jakarta State Court, Pakpahan said he wanted to call 11 new witnesses to prove his innocence in the Medan riot.

"I feel the process of this case is going ahead according to the law and I am certain the Supreme Court will in the future consider what is put forward by this court to uphold justice is this state based on laws," Pakpahan told reporters.
Observers from a number of Western embassies as well as international labour organisations attended the hearing.

Pakpahan said in his opening statement the 11 new witnesses, who were not examined in his earlier trials, would show the SBSI central board had called off the 1994 strike that triggered the rioting, which he said was provoked by the military.
A member of the North Sumatra prosecutors' office, H.P Marpuang, told the court that earlier trials had found Pakpahan responsible for inciting the riots.
"We ask the court to reject the request as it has no basis in law," he said.

After the hearing, which was adjourned to Monday, Pakpahan lashed out at the government's refusal to allow him to be treated overseas after the U.S. government and European unions offered to pay for the treatment.
"It is clear I am sick. I have a blockage in an artery in my brain and a strange object in my right lung," said Pakpahan, who looked weak and was helped by officials to walk from the court.

He said the doctors at the Cikini private hospital where he has had tests and treatment had recommended he have a Lung Imagery Fluorescence Endoscopy (LIFE) test, not available in Indonesia, to determine the nature of the object.
But a team of government doctors has said Pakpahan, who was accompanied by his private doctor to Thursday's three-hour hearing, does not need treatment and is fit to stand trial.
Pakpahan, who was initially admitted with vertigo, said the government doctors told him he could be suffering from tuberculosis, a bacterial infection or a fungus, but he did not need the LIFE test.
"What I am fighting for now is for everyone to put my health first. The (subversion) trial can go ahead, but my health is my right which is guaranteed by law," Pakpahan said.
